You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write a LinkedIn post of up to 500 words about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used.

Plain prose only: no headers, no bullet points, no bold text, no em dashes. Write like a person.

=== TEXT A ===
Two years ago I spent about four months building a feature that, as far as I can tell, was used by nine people. Not nine thousand. Nine. And I think three of them were on my team testing it.

The feature was a customizable dashboard. Users could drag widgets around, pick which metrics showed up, save different layouts for different days. We had heard from a handful of customers that our default view didn't fit their workflow, and I took that and ran with it. I wrote a spec. I got design involved. We built a whole layout engine. I remember demoing it to the sales team and feeling genuinely proud of how smooth the drag and drop felt.

Then we shipped it, and nothing happened. No spike in engagement. No support tickets, good or bad. A few people opened the customization panel, moved one widget, and never came back to it.

For a while I told myself it was a discoverability problem. We added a tooltip. We added a banner. We put it in the release notes twice. Nothing changed.

What finally made it click was a call with one of the customers who had originally asked for it. I asked her why she hadn't set up her own layout. She said, and I'm paraphrasing only slightly, "I don't want to design a dashboard. I want you to know what I need to see." She had never wanted flexibility. She wanted us to be right about the default. Flexibility was what she asked for because it was the easiest thing to say when the default was wrong.

That's the lesson I keep coming back to. When someone asks for a feature, they are usually describing a solution they can imagine, not the problem they actually have. My job was to dig underneath the request, and instead I took it at face value because it was concrete and buildable and I could picture the demo.

The honest version of the story is that I was also a little bored. The default view was a hard, unglamorous problem that required looking at a lot of data and talking to a lot of people and probably ending up somewhere unsatisfying. A layout engine was fun. I could see progress every day. I let that pull me.

What I do differently now is pretty simple. Before I write a spec, I try to say the problem out loud without mentioning any solution, and I check whether the customer nods. If I can't do that, I'm not ready to build. And when a request comes in as a fully formed feature, I treat that as a signal that I haven't asked enough questions yet, not as a shortcut.

We eventually rebuilt the default view based on what people actually looked at first every morning. It took three weeks. Engagement went up noticeably. Nobody asked for customization again.

I still think about those nine users sometimes. I hope the drag and drop was nice for them.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
The feature launched on a Tuesday. By Friday, the only people who had used it were the people who built it.

We’d spent six weeks on a dashboard that let customers customize their reports. It had filters, saved views, and a tidy little export button. In the demo, everything worked.

We were proud of it.

We’d also mistaken a recurring request for a clear understanding of the problem.

Customers had told us they needed “better reporting.” We took that phrase, wrote a spec, and got to work. We asked about chart types and date ranges. We showed mockups. People said they looked good.

What we didn’t ask was: “Can you walk us through the last time you needed a report?”

After launch, we finally did.

One customer shared her screen. Every Monday, she copied three numbers into an email to her manager. She didn’t want a dashboard to explore. She wanted that email to take two minutes instead of twenty.

Our feature gave her more options and more work.

That was the part I found hardest to admit. We hadn’t built something badly. We’d built the wrong thing carefully.

We eventually replaced most of the dashboard with a scheduled summary. It was less impressive in a demo. People used it.

Since then, I’ve tried to get closer to the actual moment of need before discussing a solution. Show me the spreadsheet. Show me the workaround. Show me what happens when you don’t get this done.

I still like a good launch.

But now I’m much more interested in what someone does with the feature the following Monday.
=== END OF TEXT B ===

Answer with a single JSON object and nothing else:
{"more_ai": "A" or "B", "confidence": 1-5, "tells_A": ["short tell", ...], "tells_B": ["short tell", ...]}

tells_B: relentless short punchy sentences - uniform rhythm
didn't want dashboard / wanted email parallelism
hadn't built badly / built wrong thing parallelism
